problem: Reachability for embodiment selection (base vs arm) in mobile manipulation is computed via inverse kinematics (online or offline reachability maps), which needs prior knowledge of the robot and environment and does not work with vision-only observations.
motivation: Mobile manipulators should move the base until the goal is reachable and only then activate the arm, for safety and efficiency. Vision-based systems lack the models needed for IK, so a learned world model that can imagine future arm trajectories could replace IK-based checks.
key_idea: Define predictive reachability as whether an imagined world-model rollout under the policy reaches a positive task reward without collision, and use it as a reward to train a top-level embodiment selector in a three-level hierarchical (selector/manager/worker) model-based RL agent (MMDirector).
insight: Explicit selection trained on predictive reachability makes the arm activate only near the goal (arm selection near goal 1.0 for MMDirector vs 0.044-0.696 for Director/Dreamer in Table 'Quantitative evaluation of the selection of arm motion'). Demonstrations as goals (the DG variant) are critical, since DE and NO fail with sparse rewards, and the dense progress reward beats an exploration reward. Hierarchy beats a flat policy because subgoals help the base approach. Splitting the action spaces speeds learning, but stage interdependence lowers final success in the empty and room environments.
method: World model: RSSM (PlaNet/Director-style) encodes RGB-D and proprioception into latents and is trained with reconstruction, KL, and task-reward and collision predictors.
Predictive reachability: imagine an H=18 step rollout from a latent state with the embodiment fixed. Reachable if any predicted task reward exceeds 0.7 and all predicted collisions stay below 0.3.

Reachability reward: for the selector, arm gets +2 if reachable and -1 if not; base gets 0. The selector is trained with a critic using a weighted target whose coefficient depends on the reward-prediction loss.
Selector policy: outputs a one-hot embodiment mask from the current state and two stage goals; the mask conditions the manager and filters worker actions.

Manager policy: Director-style, outputs discrete codes decoded to latent subgoals every K=6 steps. It uses task, collision and dense progress rewards toward the final goal instead of an exploration reward.
Worker policy: goal-conditioned on subgoal and mask, outputs discrete predefined action primitives, with epsilon-greedy exploration.
Demonstrations: whole-body guided-policy-search demos are converted to two stages (base then arm), placed in the replay buffer, and stage-goal means are used as policy goals.

setting.backbone: RSSM world model + three-level hierarchical actor-critic policy (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Online RL samples in simulation plus collected demonstrations per environment (pre-training on demos only, then RL); number of demos not stated
setting.observation: RGB + depth images, proprioception, plus 2D ray observations when obstacles are present
setting.action_space: Predefined discrete action primitives for continuous movements: base forward/back and yaw, 3 arm joints
setting.privileged: none at test time (demonstrations used in training only)

numbers_note: Results are in figures (success curves) and a custom arm-selection table; there are no standard navigation benchmark numbers. The arm-selection metrics are custom.
results: MMDirector learns faster than Director and DreamerV2 and achieves high success in all four PyBullet environments. It outperforms all baselines in the obstacle-for-arm environment, but is slightly worse than Director and Dreamer in the empty and room environments. Its arm-selection-near-goal proportion is 1.0 in all environments versus 0.044-0.696 for Director/Dreamer.
limitations: Interdependence of base and arm stages and HRL non-stationarity cause lower final success than Director in the empty and room environments; the modified variant still falls short of 100%.
Predictive reachability depends on the learned policy and world model, so estimates can be unstable and cause wrong selections.
Only simple reaching tasks in simulation, no real robot, and demonstrations are needed.
